haiku-low.q1: A person runs the failover command after on-call decides. Detection only pages on-call; it never fails over automatically.
haiku-low.q2: The command stops before fencing, leaving A untouched. It continues only if on-call passes an explicit accept-data-loss override.
haiku-low.q3: Before promotion: A is fenced (active-region record set to B, A's apps stop, 30 s wait). Before B's workers start: B's database is promoted and writable. Before DNS switches: B's /healthz passes.
haiku-low.q4: Sessions are in each region's own Redis and are not replicated, so everyone signed in at failover must sign in again.
haiku-low.q5: It is never reused as primary. When A returns, it is rebuilt as a replica of B. Moving back is a separate planned switchover.
haiku-low.q6: The active-region record in the control store says B. A's apps read it every 5 s and refuse writes when it says B or is unreadable for 15 s.
haiku-low.q7: The control store, a strongly consistent key-value store outside A. The failover command writes it, and every app and worker in both regions reads the active-region record.
haiku-low.q8: Any jobs row in B's database still marked running is set back to queued. Jobs must be idempotent because reruns may repeat work.
haiku-low.q9: Rerun the command with the explicit resume flag once sure the first run stopped. Abort goes back to A only up to and including the fence; after Promote, it only goes forward.
haiku-low.q10: Clients still on A get read-only service if A is up, or errors if not, until DNS moves. Then most move within about a minute; some resolvers may be slower.
haiku-low.q11: Data lost is bounded by replay lag, which must be 30 s or less unless overridden. The lag is a lower bound; writes A accepted after B's last WAL are unknown until A is recovered.

sonnet.q1: Only a person (on-call) starts a failover by running the failover command; there is no automatic promotion. Detection (2 of 3 probes see 3 consecutive /healthz failures) only pages on-call.
sonnet.q2: If B's last recorded replay lag is over 30 s (the RPO), the command stops before fencing, leaving A untouched. It continues only if on-call passes an explicit accept-data-loss override, meaning the last seconds of writes are lost.
sonnet.q3: Before promoting B's database: the run record is taken, the lag check passed (or was overridden), A is fenced (active-region record set to B) and the command waited 30 s. Before B's workers start (scale up): B's database is promoted and writable (and jobs stuck in running were reset to queued). Before DNS points at B: B's /healthz through B's load balancer must pass (step 9), after scale-up.
sonnet.q4: Sessions are in each region's own non-replicated Redis, so they are lost. Everyone signed in at failover time must sign in again; this is accepted.
sonnet.q5: It is never reused as primary. A is rebuilt as a replica of B. Moving back is a separate planned switchover. Meanwhile A's apps read the active-region record (B) and keep refusing writes.
sonnet.q6: The fence: A's apps and workers read the active-region record in the control store every 5 s, and refuse writes when it says B or when they cannot read it for 15 s (fail closed). So a partitioned A stops itself without being reached. The command waits 30 s for this and relies on timing alone.
sonnet.q7: The control store (a small strongly consistent key-value store outside region A) holds the active-region record. The failover command writes it (sets it to B at the fence; --abort sets it back to A). Every app and worker in A and B reads it (A's every 5 s).
sonnet.q8: A's workers are fenced or dead and B's are at zero, so any jobs row in B's database still marked running is set back to queued in the fix-up step. Jobs must be idempotent, since re-runs may repeat work and work finished in A just before the loss may not have replicated.
sonnet.q9: The run record holds the last completed step. A person reads it, and once sure the first command has stopped, reruns with the explicit resume flag; steps are safe to repeat. Going back to A is possible only via --abort, allowed up to and including the fence; it sets the active-region record back to A and marks the run aborted, and A's apps resume writing themselves. After Promote the run only goes forward.
sonnet.q10: From the fence until DNS switches, writes fail everywhere. The client gets read-only service if A is up, or errors if A is down, and nothing redirects it until DNS moves. After the switch (60 s TTL) most clients move within about a minute, but some slower resolvers may take longer. If A returns, it keeps refusing writes because the record says B.
sonnet.q11: Up to 30 s (the RPO) normally. It is limited by the lag check: the command stops if B's last recorded replay lag exceeds 30 s unless on-call passes the accept-data-loss override. Replication is asynchronous, typical lag is under 5 s. The recorded lag is only a lower bound: writes A accepted after B's last WAL are unknown until A is recovered and compared.
